paper_title: Generalization Is Stability, Not Accuracy: Multi-Axis Evaluation of LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generalization in large language models (LLMs) is the ability to produce consistent and semantically stable outputs when the same input is expressed in different ways. Existing work typically evaluates generalization through aggregate accuracy on a single prompt format, task, or set of variations, which conflates robustness with overall benchmark performance. In this work, we show generalization evaluation at the level of individual examples, across multiple input variants, and across different aspects of model behavior, focusing on variability rather than reducing performance to a score that can be improved through narrow training or other ways that obfuscate generalization evaluation. Following this view, we introduce the Stability-Aware Generalization Objective (SAGO), a framework that measures how much model behavior changes for the same input under different variations and benchmarks, capturing variability across several dimensions including generation consistency, internal activations, confidence, and response mirroring. We show that many commonly used models exhibit statistically significant and consistent generalization instability: no model generalizes uniformly, behavioral axes capture independent failure modes, and cross-dataset variation can reverse model rankings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: LLMs are used in real-world systems, including search [26, 63, 42, 70], coding assistants [50, 11, 29, 66], and agentic workflows [7, 48]. In these settings, the same user intent is rarely expressed in one fixed form. request can vary in wording, length, tone, formatting, or noise while preserving the same goal and context. Accordingly, generalization is the ability of model to preserve performance across such semantically equivalent input variations [18, 52, 71]. This requirement stems from several factors; for instance, pretraining and post-training can expose model to many examples, but they cannot cover all valid ways user may express the same request [37, 56]. Yet, an aligned model should remain useful, solve tasks, refuse harmful requests, and follow its policies regardless of how the context is expressed in the input [45, 61]. Previous work studies related forms of generalization robustness, such as distribution shifts [31, 58], meaning-preserving perturbations [18, 19], and prompt sensitivity to wording, formatting, tone, input length, and input order [36, 34, 40, 51, 52, 71], together establishing that LLM behavior shifts even when task meaning is preserved. However, while these works provide important insights into robustness under specific settings and perturbations, they do not fully capture models overall generalization ability for several reasons. First, many existing evaluations focus on single domain. Although robustness in domains such as safety is important, success in one field cannot be considered evidence of generalization ability. Second, many studies evaluate only particular family of semantically equivalent rewrites, so model may appear robust because it has adapted to one variation pattern while still failing under other forms of expression. Lastly, evaluations are commonly based on aggregate benchmark scores, which can hide substantial behavioral differences at the level of individual examples. model may maintain similar overall performance because failures on some semantically equivalent variants are offset by successes on others, even though its behavior changes considerably for individual inputs. Consequently, aggregate metrics can give misleading sense of stable and reliable generalization. In this work, we address this gap by introducing the Stability-Aware Generalization Objective (SAGO), framework for evaluating LLM generalization as per-instance behavioral stability rather than aggregate benchmark performance. Instead of asking only whether model performs well on average, SAGO tests whether the model preserves its behavior when the same goal and context are expressed through semantically equivalent input variations. The framework combines multiple datasets, multiple families of input variation, and multiple behavioral axes, allowing us to capture failures that single-domain, single-perturbation, or aggregate-score evaluations can miss. For each prompt, we compare the models baseline behavior with its behavior under controlled variations and measure changes in generation consistency, internal activations, confidence and uncertainty, and response mirroring. This enables us to identify cases where model appears stable at the benchmark level while changing substantially on individual examples, or where it is robust to one type of variation but unstable under another. Using SAGO, we evaluate eleven openand closed-source LLMs across six datasets and show that generalization instability is widespread, heterogeneous, and not captured by any single metric or domain alone. Our contributions are threefold: framework for evaluating LLM generalization as per-instance stability across semantically equivalent input variations, multiple datasets, and multiple families of variation. multi-axis metric that measures behavioral change in activation geometry, generation consistency, confidence and uncertainty, and response mirroring. We treat mirroring as behavioral sensitivity that may reflect either intended alignment or unintended instability. An empirical study of eleven LLMs across six datasets showing that no model generalizes uniformly, that generation consistency is the most sensitive axis, and that content stability and response mirroring are independent dimensions of behavioral sensitivity.

sections.title: 2 Related Work and Background
sections.content: Prior work on LLM generalization robustness spans several lines, each addressing one aspect of the broader question. We organize them according to the dimensions along which generalization can be measured. Out-of-distribution robustness. first line of research measures how models behave when test data differs from training data. Domain generalization formalizes this as single number summarizing performance on held-out distribution [69]; large-scale benchmarks aggregate this gap over many domains [25, 31], and broader evaluations of trustworthiness report aggregate accuracy under such shifts [58]. These studies establish that distribution shifts degrade performance and that the degradation is meaningful at the dataset level. However, they do not ask whether model produces consistent behavior on the same input expressed in different ways, and they aggregate over examples; thus, per-instance flipping is not measurable from their reported metrics. Consistency and sensitivity under prompt-level variation. second line of work tests whether predictions remain stable when an input is rephrased without changing its meaning. This includes identifying inconsistencies in paraphrased factual queries [18] and systematic disagreement in instruction-tuned settings [51, 19]. large body of work narrows this question to specific semantic scopes, such as cross-lingual variants [15, 60, 47], social-tone shifts [65, 8, 16], and consistency for risky or harmful requests [9, 10, 24, 39, 59]. Parallel to these semantic rewrites, third line of work investigates sensitivity to surface-level choices that have no intended impact on intent, such as formatting and template selection [52, 71], in-context example ordering [36], and low-level perturbations like punctuation and whitespace [1, 27, 53]. While these studies collectively establish that LLM behavior is rarely invariant under semantically equivalent inputs, they do not provide complete evaluation of models overall generalization ability. Most works focus on single domain or single family of input variation in isolation, making it unclear whether robustness extends beyond the specific setting being evaluated, and overestimating generalization. In addition, they typically rely on aggregate performance metricssuch as mean accuracy or performance spreadto summarize behavior. This can obscure substantial per-instance instability: model may fail on some semantically equivalent variants while succeeding on others, preserving similar overall benchmark performance despite large behavioral changes at the individual-example level. Behavioral signals beyond accuracy. The signals we use as separate axes have each been developed in their own literatures. Hidden-state geometry has been used to track how internal representations shift with input changes [27]. Semantic similarity measures such as BERTScore quantify meaning preservation between generations [67], complementing lexical-overlap measures such as BLEU [46]. Token-level log-probabilities and predictive entropy are standard tools for measuring confidence and uncertainty [20, 38]. Stylistic accommodationthe degree to which model output mirrors input registerhas been studied as behavioral phenomenon in its own right [56, 6]. While mirroring is often an intended feature of instruction tuning to improve human-computer interaction, it represents core axis of behavioral sensitivity that can also manifest as unintended instability when models mirror non-semantic variations like input noise. These signals have been used individually in service of single-axis claims; combining them within single per-instance analysis has not been attempted. While exceptional large-scale benchmarks successfully evaluate across multiple datasets, variation families, and non-aggregate metrics [23], they remain restricted to single behavioral signal such as accuracy. This makes it difficult to determine whether instability is property of the model more broadly, or whether it is localized to particular datasets, variation families, behavioral axes, or individual examples. model can therefore appear stable under one evaluation view while failing under another: it may preserve average performance while changing responses for specific prompts, remain robust to one type of variation while failing under another, or show stable outputs while its confidence or internal representations shift. Thus, the missing piece is not another single robustness test, but per-instance, multi-axis evaluation that measures how different forms of behavioral instability co-occur across datasets and semantically equivalent input variations.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate instruction-tuned LLMs under the SAGO framework (Section 3), computing SGSX for each behavioral axis across all combinations of variation family, subtype, strength, and position. Our evaluation addresses three questions: whether failure modes dissociate across the six -axes; whether within-model cross-dataset variation is large enough to reverse model rankings; and whether closedsource models exhibit qualitatively distinct instability profile relative to open-source alternatives. 4.1 Experimental Setting Setup. We evaluate eight open-source instruction-tuned models spanning three families: Llama3.2-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (L-3B, L-8B) [21]; Gemma-2B-IT, Gemma-7B-IT, and Gemma-4-E4B-IT (G-2B, G-7B, G4-E4B) [55]; and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-9B (Q-1.5B, Q-7B, Q3.5-9B) [49]. We additionally evaluate three closed-source models via API: GPT-5.4 [44], Gemini-2.5-Flash (Gem-2.5F) [12], and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (Cl-S-4.6) [2]. All models use deterministic decoding (T =0); XAct and XProb are unavailable for closed-source models due to API limitations, while XEnt is computed only for GPT-5.4. Experiments run on four NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti and four GTX 1080 Ti GPUs (CUDA 12.8); closed-source evaluation uses provider APIs. We evaluate on six open-ended factual QA datasets spanning health, law, finance, politics, science, history, geography, general knowledge, and creative instruction-following: TruthfulQA [35], Natural Questions [32], Alpaca [54], SimpleQA Verified [22], TriviaQA [30], and HotpotQA [64]. All elicit paragraph-length free-form responses suitable for measurement on all four axes, ensuring that SGSX is not estimated on narrow content distribution. We sample =16 prompts per dataset, justified by the sample size ablation in Appendix D. Variation set V. The variation set (Eq. 3) instantiates three families. Social register varies prompt framing across eleven politeness levels. Surface noise applies tokenand character-level perturbations via three subtypes: spacing, punctuation, and letter casing, each at multiple strengths. Structural rewriting reorganizes the prompt via length variation and sentence-form conversion (interrogative/imperative). Strength levels and examples for all families are in Appendix A. Non-structural variants are applied at three positions {PREFIX, SUFFIX, GLOBAL}; structural variants are global by construction. Semantic preservation is guaranteed by construction for surface-noise variants; for the remaining families, we retain only prompts where all variants exceed BERTScore > 0.85 [67, 41, 5]. The data strongly support the latter. Within the Gemma family, G4-E4B records the highest generation instability in the open-source pool (-BERT: 0.178; -BLEU: 0.837), while its predecessors score substantially lower (G-2B: 0.097; G-7B: 0.084) . model representing architectural advancement is therefore less generation-stable than its predecessors, which falsifies the intuition that capability gains transfer automatically to robustness. Q3.5-9B tells the opposite story: lowest -BERT (0.080) and -BLEU (0.520) in the open-source pool, yet the highest confidence instability (-Prob: 0.088) and substantial mirroring instability (-MR: 0.441). This reversal is not incidental noise; if generation consistency and confidence were correlated proxies of the same underlying instability, such systematic inversion across models would be impossible. It implies model can be optimized, whether explicitly or as byproduct of alignment, to produce stable outputs while simultaneously becoming more uncertain or more imitative [6]. Evaluations that aggregate across these axes would assign G4-E4B and Q3.5-9B similar robustness scores, masking failure profiles that point in opposite directions and require different interventions to address. Cross-dataset variation. models instability is not fixed scalar property; rather, it depends on the content domain. For L-8B, -Cos spans 3.7 range and -MR more than doubles across the six datasets (Appendix C). This variation is large enough to reverse model rankings depending on which dataset is chosen, which means that robustness evaluation anchored to single benchmark characterizes only that domain. For deployment settings where the content distribution is not controlled, this is practical concern: model appearing stable under one evaluation may be substantially less stable in practice. Total SGSX , which pools all six datasets with equal per-prompt weight, is the appropriate summary because it averages over this domain dependence rather than fixing it.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Generalization under semantically equivalent input variation is not well described by aggregate accuracy, single robustness score, or single behavioral metric. Instability is instead structured profile over datasets, variation families, individual prompts, and behavioral axes: model stable on one axis may be unstable on another, and stability under one dataset or variation family does not imply stability elsewhere. This matters because similar benchmark-level performance can hide substantial per-instance change, preserving models average score while its responses, confidence patterns, or mirroring behavior differ across semantically equivalent versions of the same prompt. Claims about LLM generalization should therefore be scoped to the axis, domain, and variation family evaluated; robustness on one benchmark or under one perturbation type is not evidence of broadly stable representation of the users goal and context. Comparison should likewise be profile-based rather than rank-based, since one model may be preferable when content stability matters most and another when confidence stability or reduced surface mirroring does. The openversus closed-source differences further indicate that stronger models do not eliminate instability, but may shift it to different behavioral dimensions. Several limitations bound these conclusions. SAGO measures where and how much behavior changes under controlled semantically equivalent variation, but not the causal mechanisms or internal components responsible, leaving representational drift, decoding sensitivity, and mirroring entangled. Our datasets are English-only, so whether the same dissociations hold across languages, scripts, or culturally specific prompt conventions is untested. -BLEU captures lexical deviation and may reflect harmless paraphrasing, hence -BERT as meaning-level complement. The =16 operating point is validated for typical per-prompt instability, but rare or worst-case failures may require larger samples. Finally, structural variants and social-register mirroring rely on GPT-4o-mini, which may introduce stylistic bias, and limited API access restricts closed-source conclusions to the observable axes. These bounds set the agenda for future work: extending SAGO to multilingual settings, further task families, and deployment-specific domains; linking behavioral profiles to causal mechanisms through mediation analysis or activation patching [27, 3, 33], asking whether generation inconsistency, confidence drift, and response mirroring share internal components; and judging training interventions by whether gains transfer across axes, datasets, and semantically equivalent input forms, not by reduction on single axis or variation family. Taken together, SAGO re-frames generalization as stability of model behavior for the same goal and context across valid ways of expressing an input. High benchmark performance is then necessary but not sufficient: model generalizes reliably only when its behavior remains stable at the per-instance level across the domains, variation families, and behavioral axes relevant to deployment.

sections.title: D Prompt Sample Size Ablation
sections.content: To determine the minimum number of prompts sufficient for stable estimation of the per-prompt instability sX (i) (Eq. ??), we subsample {4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128} prompts without replacement from TruthfulQA [35], repeating each draw 500 times. For each subsample we compute the standard deviation of per-(F, u, s, p) group means across the sampled prompts, and track its bootstrap [13] distribution. We define the recommended as the smallest value for which the bootstrap band (P90P10) stabilizes, taking the most conservative across all models and axes. Figure 3 shows that five of six axes plateau by =16 and remain flat through =128, confirming that =16 is sufficient for stable estimation of SGSX . We therefore stopped data collection at =128 once stability was confirmed, and adopt =16 as our operating point.
